paragraphs: 3D-RAD expands medical visual question answering from predominantly two-dimensional images to three-dimensional CT scans. Its purpose is to test a wider range of diagnostic reasoning abilities than existing datasets typically cover. The questions include both open responses and answers drawn from a restricted set, allowing different forms of model behavior to be assessed.

The dataset covers six tasks: anomaly detection, image observation, medical computation, existence detection, static temporal diagnosis, and longitudinal temporal diagnosis. This variety makes the benchmark about more than recognizing visible findings. Computational questions and multiple stages of temporal analysis also test whether a model can reason about information within and across examinations.

The evaluations find limited generalization among existing vision-language models, particularly medical models and particularly on tasks involving multiple times. The authors also provide 3D-RAD-T, a training collection containing 136,195 expert-aligned examples, and report that fine-tuning on it could substantially improve performance. Together, the benchmark and training set identify difficult capabilities while providing data intended to help develop them.
neurips-2025-3d-rad-a-comprehensive-3d-r.tldr: 3D-RAD benchmarks diverse question-answering tasks on CT scans and exposes weaknesses in models’ reasoning across time.

paragraphs: AutoRedTeamer addresses a maintenance problem in language-model safety evaluation: testing methods can depend heavily on human work and fall behind newly discovered attacks. The framework automates both running adversarial tests and expanding the collection of attacks available for future evaluations. Its intended role is an evolving evaluation process rather than a fixed collection of test prompts.

Two agents divide this work. A red teaming agent turns high-level risk categories into test cases and executes them. A strategy proposer examines recent research to discover and implement additional attacks. A memory-guided selection mechanism helps choose attacks, while the modular organization supports adding new strategies without abandoning existing ones.

On HarmBench against Llama-3.1-70B, the authors report attack success rates 20% higher and computational costs 46% lower than existing approaches. They also report test-case diversity matching human-curated benchmarks. These findings support the framework’s ability to combine broader test generation with efficient execution in the evaluated settings, making continuous attack integration a central part of automated safety assessment.
neurips-2025-autoredteamer-autonomous-re.tldr: AutoRedTeamer automates adversarial evaluation with agents that run tests and continually integrate newly discovered attacks.

paragraphs: This paper seeks useful mathematical certificates for how deep networks perform beyond their training data. PAC-Bayes theory connects training performance to generalization risk, but the choice of prior can make those certificates uninformative or expensive to obtain. The authors focus on making that choice compatible with ordinary neural-network training.

Their localized prior places a soft concentration near parameter values favored during training. Rather than training a separate prior on a costly data split, they incorporate the localized prior directly into the training loss. The goal is to preserve effective parameter exploration while producing bounds tight enough to say something useful about the resulting model.

Under standard neural tangent kernel assumptions, the authors show that their bound decreases as networks become wider and datasets grow. Empirically, they evaluate image classification, language-model fine-tuning, and semantic segmentation, reporting certificates typically within three percentage points of test errors at ImageNet scale. They also provide guarantees for individual predictions, selective rejection, and robustness. The theoretical scaling claim depends on the stated assumptions; the reported tightness describes the evaluated applications.
neurips-2025-certifying-deep-network-ris.tldr: A localized PAC-Bayes prior integrated into training produces practically tight generalization certificates in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Point cloud completion reconstructs the missing portions of an object represented by a collection of three-dimensional points. Supervised methods commonly need complete objects as training targets, but those targets can be difficult to obtain. Existing self-supervised approaches reduce this dependence, yet their training data may provide too little information about complete shapes.

The proposed framework introduces a self-supervised module that explicitly learns complete structure from incomplete point clouds. That learned structure then guides the completion process, removing the need for training examples containing complete point clouds. This makes structural guidance an internally learned component of the method rather than something supplied through complete training targets.

Two forms of contrastive learning serve complementary purposes. Learning at the cluster level extracts shape features under the guidance of the reconstructed structure, while learning at the individual-instance level captures style features. The design aims to recover overall shape while retaining detail. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report significant improvements over state-of-the-art self-supervised methods, supporting the value of combining learned structural guidance with these two feature-learning objectives.
neurips-2025-complete-structure-guided-p.tldr: The framework learns complete-shape guidance from incomplete point clouds and uses two levels of contrastive learning to preserve shape and detail.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter tuning can keep consuming computation after its expected benefits have become too small for the user. This paper studies that situation within freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization, where training configurations can be paused and continued. The central objective is to decide both which configuration deserves more training and when the entire search should end.

The method expresses the user’s trade-off between performance and computational cost through a utility function, which can be estimated from preference data. A new acquisition function chooses the configuration expected to deliver the largest future utility improvement. A corresponding stopping rule aims to end the search around its maximum utility, making the stopping decision part of optimization itself.

The authors also use transfer learning to construct a specialized surrogate model that improves sample efficiency. On established benchmarks that evaluate configurations at different training budgets, the algorithm outperforms all freeze-thaw and transfer-based Bayesian optimization baselines considered. The reported benefit is a better cost-performance balance under the specified preference-based objective, rather than simply pursuing the highest possible model performance regardless of expense.
neurips-2025-cost-sensitive-freeze-thaw-.tldr: Preference-based utility guides which hyperparameter trials to continue and when further tuning is no longer worth its computational cost.

paragraphs: WiFi sensing uses small changes in wireless channel measurements to monitor human activity without physical contact. A major obstacle is generalization: datasets gathered in controlled spaces with similar hardware and separate recording sessions do not adequately represent everyday conditions. CSI-Bench addresses this problem by collecting data in varied indoor environments under natural conditions.

The dataset contains more than 461 hours of effective recordings from commercial WiFi edge devices, covering 26 indoor environments and 35 users. It includes dedicated data for fall detection, breathing monitoring, localization, and identifying motion sources. A separate jointly labeled collection combines user identity, activity, and proximity annotations, supporting models that learn several tasks together.

CSI-Bench also supplies standardized evaluation splits and baseline results for both individual tasks and multitask learning. These components make the dataset a common basis for comparing methods under realistic signal variability. Its contribution is an evaluation and development resource for more generalizable sensing systems, with health monitoring and other human-centered applications motivating the choice of tasks and collection conditions.
neurips-2025-csi-bench-a-large-scale-in-.tldr: CSI-Bench provides extensive real-world WiFi recordings and standardized evaluations for several human-monitoring tasks.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization occurs when a more capable model learns from a weaker model’s labels and nevertheless performs better than its teacher. This paper analyzes that phenomenon in a concrete nonlinear setting: a linear convolutional network provides supervision for a two-layer convolutional network with ReLU activations. The analysis follows the stronger model’s gradient descent training.

The data model contains label-related signals of different difficulty alongside noise unrelated to the labels. Within this structured setting, the authors identify data-scarce and data-abundant regimes based on signal and noise characteristics. When data are scarce, fitting the training examples can either support generalization through benign overfitting or undermine it through harmful overfitting. The analysis characterizes the boundary between those outcomes.

With abundant data, a different mechanism appears: the stronger model initially corrects errors in its teacher’s labels. Continuing training too long can then reduce performance. These results explain why surpassing a weak teacher depends on both the available data and training dynamics. They establish distinct mechanisms within the analyzed model and data assumptions, rather than a universal promise that stronger students will outperform their supervisors.
neurips-2025-from-linear-to-nonlinear-pr.tldr: A theoretical analysis shows how data availability and training duration determine whether a nonlinear student can outperform a linear teacher.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers vary substantially in their attention mechanisms and in how they encode structural position. That variety makes it difficult to know whether a successful design reflects a broadly useful principle or a particular application. This paper combines theoretical analysis with a large empirical study to connect architectural choices to both representational capability and practical performance.

The authors introduce the Generalized-Distance Transformer, which uses standard attention and incorporates several recent advances in graph Transformer design. They analyze its representation power in terms of attention and positional embeddings. This provides a shared architecture through which the consequences of those choices can be examined in finer detail.

The evaluation spans more than eight million graphs and roughly 270 million tokens, covering object detection, molecular properties, code summarization, and algorithmic reasoning outside the training distribution. The authors identify choices that perform consistently across tasks, domains, and model scales, and report strong few-shot transfer without fine-tuning. The contribution is a set of design, training, and inference insights supported by both theory and unusually broad empirical coverage.
neurips-2025-generalizable-insights-for-.tldr: The Generalized-Distance Transformer connects expressivity analysis with broad experiments to identify graph Transformer design choices that transfer across applications.

paragraphs: This paper asks how well Transformers can represent the computations needed to learn noisy linear dynamical systems from context. The focus is approximation capability: whether a specified Transformer architecture can achieve low error across a family of such systems. The analysis uses a squared-error testing criterion defined uniformly across tasks.

The first result gives an upper bound for multilayer Transformers. With logarithmic depth, these models can achieve approximation error bounds comparable to those of a least-squares estimator. This establishes a capability of sufficiently deep architectures within the studied setting, connecting their representational power to a familiar statistical estimation method.

The second result identifies a persistent error lower bound for a particular class of single-layer linear Transformers. Together, the results suggest a separation between shallow and deeper architectures for learning dynamical systems in context. The shallow-model analysis also distinguishes independent, identically distributed observations from dependent data. That distinction matters because the approximation capabilities demonstrated in one data setting need not carry over unchanged to the other.
neurips-2025-in-context-learning-of-line.tldr: Approximation bounds suggest that depth helps Transformers learn noisy linear dynamical systems in context, while a studied shallow class retains persistent error.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary scene graph generation identifies objects and their relationships beyond a fixed category list. Recognizing an object category is not enough: when several objects share that category, a model must determine which particular instances interact. The paper argues that insufficient interaction modeling creates mistaken training signals and ambiguous matching when pretrained knowledge is transferred.

The proposed ACC framework makes interaction information central to both stages. During knowledge infusion, a bidirectional interaction prompt helps generate more reliable pseudo-supervision. During knowledge transfer, interaction-guided query selection gives priority to pairs of interacting objects, reducing interference from other instances that happen to belong to the same categories.

ACC also uses interaction-consistent knowledge distillation to separate relationship-bearing foreground from background while retaining general knowledge. These components address the same instance-matching problem at different points in learning. Experiments on three benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, supporting the usefulness of interaction-centered modeling for the evaluated scene graph tasks. The broader implication is that transferring object knowledge benefits from explicitly identifying which objects participate in a relationship.
neurips-2025-interaction-centric-knowled.tldr: ACC improves open-vocabulary scene graphs by using explicit interaction information to guide training signals, object pairing, and knowledge transfer.

paragraphs: Designing a protein to interact with a receptor requires attention to both its external surface and its underlying structure. The interface must accommodate the receptor’s geometry and biochemical properties, while the resulting protein must remain physically plausible. PepBridge addresses these linked requirements through a framework that jointly designs protein surfaces and structures.

The process begins with a receptor surface represented as a three-dimensional point cloud. A denoising diffusion bridge model maps that receptor surface to a ligand surface. A subsequent diffusion model predicts the corresponding protein structure, and Shape-Frame Matching Networks align the generated surface geometry with the backbone architecture.

This sequence connects the desired interface to the structure that supports it. The integrated design is intended to encourage complementary surfaces, stable conformations, and chemical feasibility together. Validation across several protein design scenarios finds that PepBridge generates structurally viable proteins. The stated findings support the framework’s approach to joint surface and backbone generation, with the receptor’s geometry and biochemical information guiding the design from the beginning.
neurips-2025-joint-design-of-protein-sur.tldr: PepBridge generates protein surfaces and backbones together, using receptor geometry and biochemical properties to guide complementary, viable structures.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based image restoration can produce inconsistent detail and unwanted artifacts. Kernel Density Steering addresses this during inference by allowing multiple restoration samples to influence one another. Instead of treating every generated sample independently, it uses agreement among their local image patches to guide the restoration process toward more consistently supported structures.

The framework maintains an ensemble of diffusion samples, called particles. It estimates the density of their outputs patch by patch and computes directions toward regions with greater shared support. Those directions steer each particle’s patches toward local modes within the ensemble, helping move samples away from spurious solutions associated with artifacts or model imperfections.

The approach offers an explicit trade-off: generating several particles together requires more computation, but can yield better restoration quality. It needs neither model retraining nor an external verifier and can integrate with different diffusion samplers. Numerical evaluations report substantial quantitative and qualitative improvements on real-world super-resolution and image inpainting tasks, supporting collective local guidance as a way to improve restoration at inference time.
neurips-2025-kernel-density-steering-inf.tldr: Kernel Density Steering uses agreement among multiple diffusion samples to improve image restoration at the cost of additional inference computation.

paragraphs: Generating a crystal requires choosing atomic types and arranging them within a repeating three-dimensional lattice. These combine discrete choices with continuous geometry. The paper identifies complementary strengths in existing models: language models handle atomic types well, while equivariant denoising models are better suited to refining positions and lattice parameters.

CrysLLMGen combines these capabilities in a sequential generation process. A fine-tuned language model first produces atom types, atomic coordinates, and a lattice description. A pretrained equivariant diffusion model then refines the coordinates and lattice while keeping the language model’s predicted atom types fixed. This division lets the second model improve geometry without replacing the first model’s composition choices.

Across several benchmark tasks and datasets, the authors report better performance than state-of-the-art generative approaches. They describe a balance between structural and compositional validity, alongside greater stability and novelty than language-model and denoising-model alternatives. The framework also generates materials under user-defined constraints. These results support combining specialized generative strengths when material descriptions contain both categorical and geometric information.
neurips-2025-llm-meets-diffusion-a-hybri.tldr: CrysLLMGen combines language-model composition choices with diffusion-based geometric refinement to generate valid, stable, novel crystals in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: MindForge studies how embodied language-model agents can improve by learning through interaction with other agents. Its starting problem is that agents using open-weight models can struggle with basic Minecraft tasks even after domain-specific fine-tuning. The framework makes perspective taking and accumulated social experience explicit parts of the agent’s operation.

Three components support this approach: a structured representation connecting perceptions, beliefs, desires, and actions; natural communication between agents; and a memory system with multiple components. Together, these provide mechanisms for representing perspectives, exchanging knowledge, and retaining experience. The authors evaluate both instruction-based learning and fully collaborative activity in Minecraft.

In the instructive setting involving GPT-4, open-weight MindForge agents reach three times as many technology-tree milestones and collect 2.3 times as many unique items as Voyager counterparts. In collaborative settings, two initially underperforming agents improve with additional communication rounds. The authors also observe knowledge transfer between experts and novices, joint problem solving, and adaptation to unfamiliar tasks through accumulated cultural experience. These findings support social learning as a useful component of the evaluated embodied agents.
neurips-2025-mindforge-empowering-embodi.tldr: MindForge combines perspective taking, communication, and memory to help Minecraft agents learn from instruction and collaboration.

paragraphs: This paper combines three requirements for regression: learning from a stream, resisting unreliable observations, and protecting privacy. Traditional nonparametric regression methods can be poorly suited to this combination, especially when data must be processed as they arrive. The authors develop an online method that needs only one pass through the observations.

Their H-FSGD algorithm uses functional stochastic gradient descent with the Huber loss to improve robustness to outliers and heavy-tailed errors. A second version, PH-FSGD, adds local differential privacy for real-time private estimation. These versions address the robustness and privacy requirements within the same overall approach to sequential learning.

The theoretical analysis provides finite-sample convergence guarantees and identifies step-size schedules achieving optimal convergence rates. It also examines how step size and privacy budget affect convergence, connecting practical tuning decisions to statistical behavior. Experiments support the analysis and report strong robustness and privacy protection while retaining efficiency. The contribution is therefore both an online learning procedure and an account of how its central parameters govern performance under the studied conditions.
neurips-2025-online-robust-locally-diffe.tldr: H-FSGD and its private extension provide one-pass robust regression with finite-sample guarantees and guidance on learning-rate and privacy choices.

paragraphs: Graph clustering often depends on differences in how densely groups connect. This paper examines a richer model in which a vertex can have different popularity levels for connections within its cluster and across clusters. The Popularity-Adjusted Block Model therefore captures local connectivity patterns that a uniform degree adjustment across clusters does not represent.

The authors characterize the optimal clustering error rate under this model. A central finding is that recovery can remain possible even when conventional edge-density signals disappear, provided the within-cluster and between-cluster popularity coefficients differ. This identifies an additional source of separability: differences in who connects to whom can matter even without informative differences in overall density.

The richer structure also changes what a spectral representation needs to retain. With k clusters, the expected adjacency matrix can have rank from k to k squared, so using only k eigenvectors may discard useful information. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets find that spectral methods incorporating k squared eigenvectors outperform traditional spectral approaches. The theoretical and empirical results both emphasize connectivity structure beyond aggregate density.
neurips-2025-optimal-graph-clustering-wi.tldr: Under the Popularity-Adjusted Block Model, differing local popularity patterns can enable clustering even when conventional edge-density signals vanish.

paragraphs: Harmful fine-tuning can cause an aligned language model to acquire unsafe behaviors. This paper evaluates defenses intended to protect models before such tuning and finds that harmful knowledge can still be learned within a few training steps. It then investigates whether changing the model after fine-tuning can restore safer behavior.

An initial experiment finds that purely random perturbations can reduce the harmful behavior, but also damage performance on the intended fine-tuning task. Panacea develops this observation into an adaptive perturbation optimized for application after fine-tuning. Its purpose is to retain the safety benefit while avoiding the loss of useful task performance seen with random changes.

Experiments vary the proportion of harmful data, fine-tuning tasks, and language models. The authors report reductions in average harmful scores of up to 21.2% while maintaining fine-tuning performance. Their analysis also finds distinct safety coefficients across layers in different models. The results support post-fine-tuning perturbation as a way to address the evaluated attacks while preserving the task adaptation that motivated fine-tuning.
neurips-2025-panacea-mitigating-harmful-.tldr: Panacea applies an optimized perturbation after fine-tuning to reduce harmful behavior while preserving task performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Physiological recordings contain useful patterns at several time scales, but motion, drifting baselines, and other disturbances can obscure them. Their sharp peaks and changing behavior also make a fixed description difficult. PhysioWave uses a wavelet-based architecture to capture information about both timing and frequency at multiple scales.

The work introduces large pretrained models dedicated to EMG and ECG signals and reports superior performance on downstream tasks. It then combines these with a pretrained EEG model in a multimodal framework. Each signal type passes through its own branch, and learnable weights determine how the branches’ information is fused.

This organization gives each modality a dedicated representation while allowing the combined model to use their contributions together. The authors report that the framework handles low signal-to-noise ratios, variation between people, and device mismatch effectively, outperforming existing methods on multimodal tasks. The findings support multiscale representations and learned fusion for physiological analysis, with wearable monitoring and clinical applications presented as potential areas of impact.
neurips-2025-physiowave-a-multi-scale-wa.tldr: PhysioWave learns multiscale physiological representations and combines dedicated signal branches to improve single-modality and multimodal tasks.

paragraphs: Training a foundation model on several datasets requires deciding how often to sample each source. PiKE approaches that choice as a multitask learning problem. Its motivation is the observation that large multilingual or multidomain pretraining often exhibits little gradient conflict, meaning updates associated with different tasks do not strongly oppose one another.

Rather than keeping sampling proportions fixed, PiKE adjusts them throughout training using these non-conflicting gradient interactions. Its weighting rule is derived from a near-tight bound governing the average loss change at each step. The authors report negligible computational overhead, making the adaptation intended to fit within large-scale training rather than becoming a substantial additional workload.

The paper provides convergence guarantees and extends the method to encourage more balanced learning across tasks. In large-scale language-model pretraining experiments, PiKE converges faster and improves downstream performance compared with existing approaches, including static and non-adaptive mixtures. The findings support adapting data allocation to useful interactions between tasks in the low-conflict setting that motivates the method.
neurips-2025-pike-adaptive-data-mixing-f.tldr: PiKE dynamically adjusts training-data mixtures using non-conflicting gradient interactions, improving convergence and downstream results in large-scale pretraining experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies language models as translators from compiler intermediate representations to assembly code. Two obstacles motivate the work: a shortage of dedicated benchmarks and difficulty producing code that is both correct and fast. NeuComBack supplies a benchmark and evaluation workflow for measuring these capabilities across recent frontier models.

The authors also introduce a prompt optimization method that learns from previous self-debugging traces. By extracting lessons from those traces, a model iteratively revises its prompting strategies for future compilation attempts. The method aims to make accumulated debugging experience useful beyond the individual program that originally produced it.

Compared with baseline prompts, reported functional correctness increases from 44% to 64% on x86_64 and from 36% to 58% on aarch64. Among 16 correctly generated x86_64 programs produced by the method, 14 run faster than clang-O3 outputs. That performance result concerns the correctly generated subset. Improvements across both architectures and the benchmark’s L1 and L2 distributions support the value of evolving prompts through debugging experience for the evaluated compilation tasks.
neurips-2025-qimeng-neucomback-self-evol.tldr: NeuComBack benchmarks neural compilation, while a debugging-informed prompt optimization method improves assembly correctness and performance in the reported tests.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs can supply external information to machine-learning systems through vector representations of their entities. Existing embedding methods, however, often focus on predicting missing links rather than producing features for other tasks. Their memory requirements also make applying them to very large graphs an engineering challenge.

SEPAL addresses both issues by optimizing embeddings for only a small core of entities, then spreading those representations through the remaining graph with message passing. The design aims to maintain global consistency across embeddings while limiting the portion of the graph requiring direct optimization. This makes propagation central to both representation quality and scalability.

The authors evaluate the method on seven large knowledge graphs and 46 downstream machine-learning tasks. They report significant improvements over previous methods on those tasks, alongside the ability to scale the underlying embedding model to huge graphs on commodity hardware. These findings support judging graph embeddings by their usefulness as external features, and show how a core-and-propagation strategy can make that objective practical at larger scales.
neurips-2025-scalable-feature-learning-o.tldr: SEPAL learns embeddings on a small graph core and propagates them outward, improving downstream features while scaling to huge knowledge graphs.

paragraphs: Data attribution estimates how individual training examples influence a machine-learning model. This paper examines a practical complication: the attribution method’s own settings can substantially affect its results. A large empirical study finds that most common methods are sensitive to particular hyperparameters, making careful selection important for their use.

Ordinary model tuning often relies on inexpensive validation measurements. Evaluating attribution quality, by contrast, can require retraining models on different subsets of the training data. Repeating that procedure across candidate settings makes conventional hyperparameter search costly, so the paper argues for using theoretical understanding to guide more efficient selection.

As a concrete case study, the authors analyze the regularization term used in many influence-function methods. That analysis leads to a lightweight procedure for choosing the regularization value without retraining the model, which they validate on standard attribution benchmarks. The contribution combines evidence of a broad sensitivity problem with a targeted solution for one important setting, showing why attribution methods should specify how their hyperparameters are selected.
neurips-2025-taming-hyperparameter-sensi.tldr: The paper reveals widespread hyperparameter sensitivity in data attribution and derives a retraining-free way to select regularization for influence-function methods.

paragraphs: An agent can spend extra computation reasoning before an action, but that alone does not give it new observations from its environment. This paper studies another resource: allowing more interaction within a single rollout. A longer interaction horizon creates opportunities to explore, revisit earlier decisions, and revise plans as new information arrives.

The study focuses on web agents and first finds that prompting alone can make expanded interaction improve task success. The authors then introduce TTI, an online reinforcement-learning approach with a curriculum that adaptively adjusts interaction lengths during training rollouts. This trains agents to use additional interaction opportunities as part of their behavior.

Using Gemma 3 12B, TTI achieves the best reported results on WebVoyager and WebArena among open-source agents trained on public data. Case studies show agents adaptively balancing exploration with pursuing promising actions. The results support interaction length as a useful complement to computation spent on each action, with the evaluated gains coming from learning how to engage with the environment over a longer sequence.
neurips-2025-thinking-vs-doing-improving.tldr: TTI trains web agents to use longer, adaptive interactions, improving benchmark success through exploration, backtracking, and replanning.

paragraphs: TRAP examines whether visually natural image changes can bias the choices of agents powered by vision-language models. The concern is semantic: an image can influence how an agent interprets candidates and makes a selection, even when the manipulation does not appear as an obvious visual disturbance. The framework does not require access to model internals.

Its generative approach uses diffusion-based semantic manipulation, combining negative-prompt degradation with positive semantic optimization. A Siamese semantic network guides the process, while spatial masking accounts for layout. These components aim to produce natural-looking images that redirect preferences through the connection between visual content and language-based interpretation.

The authors construct multiple-candidate decision scenarios using COCO and test models including LLaVA-34B, Gemma3, GPT-4o, and Mistral-3.2. They report consistent preference redirection and stronger results than SPSA, Bandit, and standard diffusion baselines. The findings identify a vulnerability in the evaluated agents’ cross-modal decisions and motivate defenses that account for semantic influence as well as resilience to pixel-level changes.
neurips-2025-trap-targeted-redirecting-o.tldr: TRAP uses natural-looking semantic image manipulations to redirect vision-language agents’ choices without accessing their model internals.

paragraphs: Language-model outputs can change when evaluation batch size, GPU count, or hardware type changes, even with greedy decoding. This paper investigates the numerical origin of that instability. In limited-precision arithmetic, regrouping operations can change their rounded results, allowing seemingly incidental system configurations to affect generated responses.

The effect is especially consequential for reasoning models, where a small difference in an early token can lead to a different subsequent reasoning sequence. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B under bfloat16 precision, the authors report up to 9% variation in accuracy and differences of 9,000 response tokens across configurations. Controlled experiments examine when outputs diverge across hardware, software, and numerical precision settings.

The proposed mitigation, LayerCast, stores model weights in 16-bit precision while performing all computations in FP32. This separates the memory savings of lower-precision storage from the numerical stability of higher-precision arithmetic. The work makes precision an explicit part of reproducible evaluation and presents a lightweight inference pipeline intended to balance those two requirements.
neurips-2025-understanding-and-mitigatin.tldr: Limited-precision arithmetic can destabilize LLM evaluations across system configurations; LayerCast combines 16-bit weight storage with FP32 computation to improve stability.
